teaser.text: Yum! Brands is a restaurant company built around KFC, Taco Bell and Habit Burger & Grill. Its central business is not only selling meals, but also letting other businesses sell those meals under Yum’s names.

stock.title: Yum stock forecast
stock.meta_description: Yum's stock forecast weighs Taco Bell traffic, franchisee health, debt and Pizza Hut proceeds across bear, base and bull scenarios.
stock.opening: Yum's weighted forecast is $141.19 in October 2027 and reaches $173.75 in October 2029. It hinges on Taco Bell traffic, franchisee economics, debt refinancing and the use of Pizza Hut proceeds.
stock.closing: The full memo also explains Yum's business, its rivals, its management and its risks.

blocks.heading: Where could Yum's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The weighted forecast starts below today’s price but improves as Yum’s earnings and buybacks compound. The weighted price is $141.19 in October 2027, a 4% total loss including dividends. It reaches $156.79 in October 2028, an 8% gain, and $173.75 in October 2029, a 22% gain. The October 2029 range runs from $91.80 in the bear case to $263.30 in the bull case. Today’s reference price is $150.51.

The base case is the most likely path at 53%, followed by the bear case at 27% and the bull case at 20%. The wide range reflects uncertainty over Taco Bell traffic, franchisee economics, debt refinancing and how aggressively Yum uses Pizza Hut proceeds.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Yum?

paragraphs.text: The bear case holds earnings at $1,802 million through October 2028 before a small recovery to $1,824 million. It assumes weak Taco Bell traffic, discounting and lower franchisee returns. The bull case reaches $2,010 million first, then $2,232 million and $2,475 million as Taco Bell recovers, KFC expands profitably and Byte improves productivity. Continuing-brand system sales grew 7% and core operating profit grew 8% in the second quarter of 2026, supporting upside, but the latest earnings also contained a $359 million tax benefit that is excluded from all cases.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Yum really make?

paragraphs.text: Working capital explains why cash and profit can diverge. Royalties may be recognized before Yum collects them, while tax timing and employee payments can shift cash between periods. Stock compensation creates another gap: Yum paid $70 million in stock-based pay in 2025. It is added back to operating cash, but shareholders bear dilution or the cost of repurchases.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Yum today?

paragraphs.text: The P/E ratio means price divided by earnings per share. A trailing P/E uses recent reported earnings; a forward P/E uses expected earnings. The forward multiple can be higher even when the share price is unchanged because its earnings denominator is smaller. That may reflect the loss of Pizza Hut’s profits or the removal of unusual benefits, rather than a sudden collapse in the restaurants.

blocks.heading: How much does Yum pay in dividends per share?

paragraphs.text: The base dividend rises from $3.12 per share to $3.24 and then $3.36. That is roughly 4% annual growth, below the recent record, because debt and buybacks compete for cash. The bear case holds the dividend at $3.00 annually, preserving the current quarterly rate. The bull case reaches $3.20, $3.48 and $3.76 as stronger free cash flow supports larger increases. Yum generated $1,639 million of free cash flow in 2025, but net debt was $11,601 million at June 2026.

blocks.heading: Does Yum's dividend fit its cash flow?

paragraphs.subsection: 5.7 — Franchise mix, leverage and capital allocation
paragraphs.text: Capital allocation puts pressure on the cash model. In 2025, Yum paid approximately $789 million in dividends and spent $552 million repurchasing shares. Buybacks can increase EPS by reducing the share count, but they do not improve a restaurant or reduce franchisee debt. Management later acknowledged that first-half repurchases used both free cash flow and revolver borrowing.

paragraphs.text: The forecast would move toward the bear case if Taco Bell traffic remains weak through October 2027–2028, discounting damages margins, or franchisee cash returns delay openings during 2028 and 2029. Refinancing pressure or an adverse tax outcome would further reduce buyback capacity and could compress the multiple.

earnings.title: Yum earnings date and guidance
earnings.meta_description: Yum reports on November 3, 2026; watch Taco Bell traffic, restaurant margin and debt refinancing.
earnings.opening: Yum’s next results are expected on November 3, 2026. The main thing to watch is Taco Bell traffic and margin recovery.
earnings.closing: The full memo also covers Yum’s business, rivals, management and risks.

paragraphs.text: Management targets 5% restaurant growth and 7% system-sales growth. It targets at least 8% core operating-profit growth. For 2026, guidance calls for $400 million of gross capital expenditure and $50 million of refranchising proceeds. Refranchising means selling company-run restaurants to independent operators who pay brand fees. Net capital expenditure is $350 million.

blocks.heading: How have Yum revenue and profit trended?

paragraphs.text: The June 2026 quarter delivered operating growth, but its earnings increase was largely tax-driven. Revenue rose 12.2% from the prior-year quarter, while operating income rose 5.3%, so sales grew faster than operating profit.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Yum’s next results?

paragraphs.text: Yum is due to discuss third-quarter results on November 3, 2026. For the September quarter, management forecast U.S. company-restaurant margins of 19.0%–21.0%. Restaurant margin is the share of sales left after restaurant operating expenses, before corporate costs and other charges. The test is whether returning customers restore that margin without sustained discounting.

The food-safety outbreak was declared over in September, but customer traffic remained an open question. From July 6 through September 11, 2026, Taco Bell visits were 12.2% below the comparable prior-year period. Visits are not sales, because prices and order sizes can change, but the decline keeps customer confidence and promotional costs in focus.
